# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

[Learn About the Roman Telescope Launch about NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)

### Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launch

NASA’s next great spaceborne observatory rocketed into the sky above Florida at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, beginning a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit. There the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for NASA’s first chief astronomer, will open a deep, panoramic view of the cosmos, generating unprecedented images that will revolutionize our understanding of the universe.

### ‘We Are Seekers’ — And We Have Confirmed More Than 6,000 Worlds Beyond Our Own

The oﬃcial number of exoplanets — planets outside our solar system — confirmed by NASA has reached (and then quickly exceeded) 6,000. The first exoplanet around a Sun-like star was discovered 30 years ago. Since then, the number has rapidly increased as technologies improve.  
  
Thousands more candidate planets await confirmation, and each confirmed planet enables scientists to learn more about the conditions under which planets can form, how common planets like Earth might be, and where to look for them.

# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

[Learn About the Roman Telescope Launch about NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)

### Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launch

NASA’s next great spaceborne observatory rocketed into the sky above Florida at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, beginning a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit. There the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for NASA’s first chief astronomer, will open a deep, panoramic view of the cosmos, generating unprecedented images that will revolutionize our understanding of the universe.

Is our home — our solar system — unique among all the systems of stars and their companion planets in the Milky Way galaxy? When compared to other planetary systems, are we that different? # Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

[Learn About the Roman Telescope Launch about NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasas-dark-universe-seeking-nancy-grace-roman-space-telescope-launches/)

### Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Launch

NASA’s next great spaceborne observatory rocketed into the sky above Florida at 7:26 a.m. EDT Sunday, Aug. 30, beginning a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit. There the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, named for NASA’s first chief astronomer, will open a deep, panoramic view of the cosmos, generating unprecedented images that will revolutionize our understanding of the universe.

Is our home — our solar system — unique among all the systems of stars and their companion planets in the Milky Way galaxy? When compared to other planetary systems, are we that different? # Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.

# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.

# Exoplanets

An exoplanet is any planet beyond our solar system. Most of them orbit other stars, but some free-floating exoplanets, called rogue planets, are untethered to any star. We’ve confirmed more than 6,000 exoplanets, out of the billions that we believe exist.

## Overview

Most of the exoplanets discovered so far are in a relatively small region of our galaxy, the Milky Way. (“Small” meaning within thousands of light-years of our solar system; one light-year equals 5.88 trillion miles, or 9.46 trillion kilometers.) Even the closest known exoplanet to Earth, [Proxima Centauri b](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/proxima-centauri-b/), is still about 4 light-years away. We know there are more planets than stars in the galaxy.

By measuring exoplanets’ sizes (diameters) and masses (weights), we can see compositions ranging from rocky (like Earth and Venus) to gas-rich (like Jupiter and Saturn). Some planets may be dominated by water or ice, while others are dominated by iron or carbon. We’ve identified [lava worlds](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/55-cancri-b/) covered in molten seas, puffy planets the [density of Styrofoam](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/kepler-7b/) and dense [cores of planets](https://science.nasa.gov/exoplanet-catalog/psr-b125712-b/) still orbiting their stars.

## NASA Launches ‘Discovery Machine,’ the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope

This flagship mission set sail Sunday, Aug. 30, to open a new era of unprecedented cosmic surveys. Its crisp, panoramic view of space combined with fast survey speeds will give astronomers a chance to study the universe as never before. Its launch from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida began a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbit; once there, “Roman will be a discovery machine,” said NASA Science head Nicky Fox, bringing us “closer than ever before to answering humanity’s most profound questions about our cosmic history.”   
When it begins its work in early 2027, Roman will help astronomers explore [dark matter](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-matter/), [dark energy](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/dark-energy/), and [worlds outside of our solar system](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/roman-space-telescope/exoplanets/), known as exoplanets.   
In three decades of discovery, scientists have so far confirmed 6,300+ exoplanets in our galaxy; Roman is expected to discover 100,000 more.
